title: Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus
author: Qianyue Hao · Fengli Xu · Yong Li · James Evans

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s account with large-scale evidence from science that AI-associated individual productivity gains can coincide with narrower collective inquiry, smaller teams and fewer junior participants. This supports concern that immediate gains may reconfigure work and weaken developmental pipelines, although it does not directly establish legal competence effects or causation.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s proposition with large-scale evidence from natural science: AI adoption is associated with substantial individual productivity and impact gains, yet its benefits concentrate in data-rich topics and coincide with narrower collective exploration. This reinforces the distinction between local performance gains and broader organisational or system-level value, while showing that selective deployment can reshape what work is pursued—not merely how efficiently it is performed.
qs: Generally, these results highlight an emerging conflict between individual and collective incentives to adopt AI in science, where scientists receive expanded personal reach and impact, but the knowledge extent of entire scientific fields tends to shrink and focus attention on a subset of topical areas.

Notably, the correlation of AI-use with frequency of mentioned data resources rises with the size and intensity of AI-models from 0.24 in the machine learning era to 0.36 in the deep learning era to 0.43 in the large model era.

st.t: Scientific adoption: Established methods persist beside AI
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster: its tables show method rankings changing across eras while established techniques persist, and recent field-specific rankings place LLMs alongside—not uniformly ahead of—CNNs, SVMs, random forests and other methods. It also confirms that the supplied excerpts establish adoption rankings rather than effects on scientific impact or research breadth.

kp.k: Large-scale natural-science evidence contrasts individual and collective benefits
kp.d: Hao, Xu, Li and Evans analyse 41,298,433 OpenAlex papers spanning 1980–2025 in biology, medicine, chemistry, physics, materials science and geology. Their domain is scientific research, not legal services. They exclude computer science and mathematics to focus on adoption rather than development of AI methodologies. The central finding is an association between greater individual productivity and career advancement and narrower collective scientific exploration.
qs: Using a dataset of 41.3 million research papers across natural science and covering distinct eras of AI, here we show an accelerated adoption of AI tools among scientists and consistent professional advantages associated with AI usage, but a collective narrowing of scientific focus.

kp.k: Identified AI adoption accelerates across three technological eras
kp.d: A two-stage, fine-tuned BERT ensemble classifies titles and abstracts, identifying 310,957 AI-augmented papers, or 0.75% of selected papers. Validation on 1,320 papers labelled by three experts each produces an overall F1-score of 0.875 and Fleiss’ Kappa of 0.964. Methods define machine learning as 1980–2014, deep learning as 2015–2022 and generative AI as 2023–present. The authors report progressively faster adoption by papers and researchers, while acknowledging that classification misses subtle or undisclosed AI use.
qs: In total, we identify 310,957 AI-augmented papers, comprising 0.75% of all selected papers.
The BERT model attains an F1-score of 0.875 in an evaluation that uses the expert labels as ground truth.
Meanwhile, the growth rate of AI papers and AI researchers in all disciplines increased progressively from the ML to the DL and generative AI eras

kp.k: AI adopters exhibit substantially higher productivity and citation impact
kp.d: Across the main comparisons, AI-adopting researchers annually publish 3.02 times as many papers and receive 4.84 times as many citations as non-adopters. Analysis of 27,405,011 papers with intact reference records finds AI papers receive 98.70% higher annual citations on average. Citation advantages persist after excluding reviews and other special publications and among continuously publishing researchers. These are observational comparisons, not fully identified causal effects.
qs: Scientists who engage in AI-augmented research publish 3.02 times more papers, receive 4.84 times more citations, and become research project leaders 1.37 years earlier than those who do not.
annual citations to AI papers are 98.70% higher than non-AI papers on average

kp.k: Matched careers show smaller but persistent adopter advantages
kp.d: To examine selection into AI adoption, the authors compare 11,019 scientists adopting AI in career year three with 1,926 non-adopters exhibiting comparable early citation trajectories. By year ten, adopters have 24.45% higher annual citations; a productivity-matched comparison finds 9.61% higher annual productivity. A second cohort of 9,837 fifth-year adopters shows the same pattern. The authors interpret these comparisons as suggesting AI contributes to subsequent advantages, while retaining their overall causal qualification.
qs: By the tenth year of their careers, the scientists who adopted AI in their third year have 24.45% higher annual citations than their non-AI-adopting counterparts with similar early trajectories.
Similarly, their annual productivity in the tenth year is 9.61% higher than the matched group of non-AI-adopters with comparable early-career productivity.

kp.k: AI research teams contain disproportionately fewer junior scientists
kp.d: AI-augmented teams average 1.33 fewer scientists, a 19.29% difference from non-AI teams. Junior membership averages 1.99 rather than 2.89, a 31.14% reduction, whereas established membership averages 3.58 rather than 4.01, a 10.77% reduction. The authors identify a disproportionately smaller junior component within an overall trend towards larger scientific teams; this is a team-composition finding rather than a direct measurement of eliminated jobs.
qs: The results reveal that AI-augmented research is associated with reduced research team sizes, averaging 1.33 (19.29%) fewer scientists
Specifically, the average number of junior scientists decreased from 2.89 in non-AI teams to 1.99 (31.14%) in AI teams
while the number of established scientists decreased from 4.01 to 3.58 (10.77%) in AI teams

kp.k: Adopting juniors reach research leadership earlier
kp.d: Using 2,282,029 career trajectories, the study defines established scientists through having been a paper’s last author, treated as project leadership. A fitted birth-death model estimates transition times of 7.33 years for AI adopters versus 8.70 years for non-adopters, a 1.37-year difference. The reported transition probability for AI-adopting juniors is 45.00%, described as 13.64% higher than for non-adopters, although the accompanying discipline-level tests report p<0.2 in four of six disciplines. Career exit is inferred from publication inactivity, with robustness checks using two- and four-year thresholds around the principal three-year threshold.
qs: Here, we define the project leader as the last author of a research paper
We find that the anticipated transition time to becoming established scientists is 1.37 years shorter for AI-adopted junior scientists compared to their counterparts.
The expectation of transition time is 7.33 years for junior scientists adopting AI

kp.k: Career benefits vary across demographic groups
kp.d: Supplementary analyses report weaker associations between AI adoption and reduced publication-based dropout for researchers in Africa and South America than in Asia-Pacific and North America, and less pronounced benefits for Black researchers than White and Asian or Pacific Islander researchers. Female researchers exhibit higher baseline dropout and smaller associated benefits than males. Institutional attributes come from OpenAlex, while gender and ethnicity are inferred from names. The authors explicitly frame these findings as preliminary and leave their causes and consequences for further investigation.
qs: Male researchers tend to have lower original dropout probabilities and receive greater benefit from AI adoption.
In contrast, female researchers exhibit higher original dropout probabilities and gain relatively less from adopting AI.
These findings provide preliminary evidence regarding the heterogeneous impact of AI on scientific careers across different demographic groups

kp.k: AI research occupies a narrower collective knowledge space
kp.d: SPECTER 2.0 embeds papers in 768 dimensions. Knowledge extent is operationalised as the maximum distance from a sampled set’s centroid, described by the authors as its 'diameter'; equal-sized samples of 1,000 AI and non-AI papers are compared across 1,000 repetitions. AI research has 4.63% lower median collective knowledge extent, consistently across six disciplines and in more than 70% of over 200 subfields. Lower knowledge entropy also indicates concentration. These measures concern embedded topical breadth rather than a literal count of scientific topics lost.
qs: Compared to conventional research, AI research is associated with a 4.63% contracted median collective knowledge extent across science
the contraction of knowledge extent can be observed in more than 70% of sub-fields
indicating an increasingly disproportionate focus on specific problems rather than across entire fields.

kp.k: Data abundance correlates increasingly strongly with AI adoption
kp.d: The authors proxy topic-level data abundance through normalised frequencies of data-related terms in titles and abstracts. Its correlation with AI adoption rises from 0.24 in the machine-learning era to 0.36 in deep learning and 0.43 in the large-model era. They interpret data availability as an important mechanism concentrating research. Measured original citation impact, disruption and funding priority have absolute Pearson correlations below 0.1 with adoption. Stratifying potential confounders into ten tiers leaves the knowledge-extent contraction evident within each tier.
qs: Notably, the correlation of AI-use with frequency of mentioned data resources rises with the size and intensity of AI-models from 0.24 in the machine learning era to 0.36 in the deep learning era to 0.43 in the large model era.
In general, data abundance is a major external factor influencing the selectivity of AI adoption across different topics

kp.k: Broader individual influence coexists with weaker follow-on engagement
kp.d: AI papers’ citation families span 3.46% more knowledge space on average, so collective narrowing is not attributed to narrower reach from each original paper. However, follow-on engagement—the proportion of possible citation links actually present among papers citing the same original work—is 22.00% lower. The authors interpret this as star-like attention around prominent works rather than dense, interconnected research development. Engagement here measures citation structure, not direct interpersonal collaboration.
qs: the knowledge extent of AI papers’ citation families is on average 3.46% more expanded compared to non-AI papers’
Results demonstrate AI research spawns 22.00% less follow-on engagement
This results in a star-like structure around specific popular research topics, rather than a network of emergent and interconnected research works.

kp.k: Recognition concentrates around superstar papers and potentially overlapping work
kp.d: Among AI papers, the top 22.20% receive 80% of citations and the top 54.14% receive 95%; citation Gini is 0.754 versus 0.690 for non-AI papers. Across 590,325,130 pairs citing a common original paper, disengaged pairs have 18.11% greater median embedding distance, but the closest disengaged pairs are 76.51% closer than the closest engaged pairs. The authors interpret these patterns as suggesting occasional overlapping work among mutually unaware researchers, rather than directly establishing duplication for every close pair.
qs: with 22.20% of top papers receiving 80% of the citations and the top 54.14% receiving 95% of citations.
This unequal distribution leads to a GINI coefficient of 0.754 in citation patterns surrounding AI research, higher than 0.690 for non-AI papers
Occasionally, however, due to the lack of reciprocal engagement, it is possible that mutually-unaware papers lie very close to each other, which indicates more overlapping research.

kp.k: Higher visibility need not imply more disruptive discovery
kp.d: Supplementary analysis finds lower disruption scores for AI papers despite higher citation counts, which the authors interpret as developing existing fields rather than initiating new ones. They describe collective attention as favouring solutions to known problems over generation of new questions. They nevertheless acknowledge that concentrated and overlapping research can support replication, extension and practical solutions; the concern about becoming fixed on local maxima is an interpretation of the observed patterns.
qs: Despite higher citation counts for AI papers, we find that their disruption scores are lower.
the higher impact is primarily developmental rather than disruptive
It is true that more overlapping attention and a contracted focus may benefit scientific replication and extension, accelerating the emergence of solid and practical solutions to specific questions.

kp.k: Robustness checks support patterns without establishing causality
kp.d: The authors report consistent results in 23,576,370 OpenAlex papers linked to Web of Science, after dimensional reduction and with cosine rather than Euclidean distances. Nevertheless, they explicitly cannot fully identify causal links between adoption and impact. Classification misses subtle or unmentioned use, and the natural-science focus limits generalisation to other domains. The findings therefore remain qualified observational evidence rather than proof that AI alone causes career gains or collective narrowing.
qs: Our identification approach, though validated by experts, misses subtle and unmentioned forms of AI use, and our focus on natural sciences excludes important domains where AI adoption patterns may differ.
Moreover, despite consistently suggestive evidence, we cannot fully identify the causal linkage between AI adoption and scientific impact.
23,576,370 could be linked to a WOS publication.

kp.k: Generative-era findings remain preliminary, excluding career-transition replication
kp.d: The separate generative-era analysis covers 4,797,614 publications and reports patterns consistent with earlier periods for impact, knowledge extent and engagement. It is a publication-period subset, while the wider study primarily concerns decades of conventional machine learning and deep learning. Limited elapsed time and publication delays constrain interpretation; the authors cannot separately replicate career-transition analysis and call for further evaluation as generative models evolve and richer longitudinal data emerge.
qs: 4,797,614 are published in the generative AI era.
Therefore, we are not able to replicate the analysis regarding the career development of individual scientists.
results in the generative AI era may appear less significant than corresponding results in our general findings and serve as a starting point for future research

kp.k: Expand experimental capacity rather than only analyse existing data
kp.d: The authors recommend developing AI that expands sensory and experimental capabilities, enabling collection of new data in previously inaccessible domains rather than primarily processing existing datasets. They warn that individual incentives and increased support for AI science could divert attention from foundational, data-poor questions towards operational, data-rich problems. This is a proposed policy and technical direction for preserving exploration, not an evaluated intervention.
qs: This could shift collective attention away from new and original questions that lack the data required for AI to demonstrate benefit.
enabling scientists to search, select, and gather new types of data from previously inaccessible domains rather than merely optimizing analysis of standing data.
Expanding the scope of AI’s deployment in science will be required for sustained scientific research and to stimulate new fields rather than merely automate existing ones.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hao, Xu, Li and Evans claim that AI adoption in natural science is accelerating and is associated with greater individual productivity, visibility and faster career progression.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about science, not legal services. The authors identify 310,957 AI-augmented papers, or 0.75% of their selected corpus. Across 1980–2025, the share of AI papers increased between 10.70-fold and 51.89-fold across disciplines, while the proportion of AI-adopting researchers increased between 135.46-fold and 362.16-fold. They report that AI adopters publish 3.02 times as many papers annually and receive 4.84 times as many citations as non-adopters; AI papers receive 98.70% more annual citations on average. Their career model estimates transition to research leadership at 7.33 years for adopters versus 8.70 for non-adopters, a 1.37-year difference. They also associate adoption with greater likelihood of becoming established and lower likelihood of leaving academia. These are empirical associations and model-based estimates, although some passages use causal language.

pts.k: The authors associate AI research with smaller teams, particularly fewer junior scientists, despite better career outcomes for individual adopters.
pts.d: AI research teams average 1.33 fewer scientists, a 19.29% difference. Average junior membership is 1.99 in AI teams versus 2.89 in non-AI teams, a 31.14% difference; established membership is 3.58 versus 4.01, a 10.77% difference. The authors interpret this as a change concentrated in junior participation. The reported comparison concerns team composition, not a measured number of jobs eliminated or a forecast of aggregate scientific employment.

pts.k: The authors argue that individual gains coexist with a narrower collective research focus, less follow-on engagement and more concentrated recognition.
pts.d: They report 4.63% lower median collective knowledge extent for AI research, consistent across six disciplines and present in more than 70% of over 200 subfields, alongside lower knowledge entropy. Conversely, individual AI paper families span 3.46% more knowledge extent on average. Follow-on engagement is 22.00% lower, and citation inequality is higher: a Gini coefficient of 0.754 versus 0.690 for non-AI research, with the top 22.20% of AI papers receiving 80% of citations. Embedding distances among papers without mutual citation suggest occasional overlapping research. Lower disruption scores are interpreted as development of existing fields rather than initiation of new ones. The authors describe a tension between personal advancement and collective exploration, rather than claiming that every AI paper covers fewer topics.

pts.k: The authors identify data availability as a likely driver of concentration and warn that continued incentives could divert science from new, data-poor questions.
pts.d: Their proposed mechanism is that AI disproportionately attracts research toward data-rich areas, encouraging solutions to known problems rather than generation of new questions. They report that AI penetration correlates with their data-abundance proxy at 0.24 in the machine-learning era, 0.36 in the deep-learning era and 0.43 in the large-model era. They find little relationship with the measured alternatives of prior impact and funding priority and argue that inherent topicality does not explain the pattern. Looking forward, they warn that expanded support for AI science combined with individual rewards could deepen concentration on local maxima. They qualify this warning by acknowledging potential benefits for replication, extension and practical solutions. Their proposed remedy is AI that expands sensory and experimental capabilities to gather new kinds of data. This is a conditional policy argument, not a dated or quantified forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a large observational bibliometric study with expert-validated AI classification, citation and career analyses, and reported robustness checks.
pts.d: The authors analyse 41,298,433 OpenAlex papers in six natural-science disciplines. A two-stage fine-tuned BERT title-and-abstract ensemble identifies AI use. Twelve experts label 1,320 papers, three experts per paper; agreement is Fleiss’ kappa 0.964, and classifier F1 is 0.875. Citation analyses use 27,405,011 papers with intact reference records; career-transition analysis uses 2,282,029 trajectories. A matched comparison of 11,019 third-year adopters with 1,926 non-adopters having comparable early citation trajectories finds 24.45% higher annual citations in career year ten; the corresponding productivity comparison finds 9.61% higher output. A fifth-year adoption cohort yields a similar pattern. The authors also report consistency for continuously publishing researchers, alternative dropout thresholds, original-research-only samples, and a 23,576,370-paper subset linked to Web of Science. They explicitly acknowledge that these analyses do not fully identify causality.

pts.k: The collective-focus and mechanism claims rely on operational proxies, while the long-term policy warning is an interpretation of those findings.
pts.d: Knowledge extent is calculated from 768-dimensional SPECTER 2.0 paper embeddings. Although called a 'diameter', its operational definition is the maximum Euclidean distance from a sampled set’s centroid. Each domain comparison samples 1,000 AI and 1,000 non-AI papers and repeats this 1,000 times. Engagement is the ratio of actual citations among papers citing a common focal paper to the maximum possible citations among them; it is not a direct measure of interpersonal collaboration. Data abundance is proxied by normalized frequencies of terms such as 'data' and 'dataset', not a direct inventory of available datasets. Overlap is inferred from embedding proximity among non-engaged papers. The authors report robustness to dimensionality reduction, cosine distance and stratification by potential confounders. Their recommendation for new sensory and experimental capacity also draws on cited robotic-science examples and historical arguments; they do not directly test that intervention.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings mainly concern decades of conventional AI; evidence specific to the recent generative-AI era is preliminary and cannot establish generative-AI career effects.
pts.d: The corpus spans 1980–2025, using OpenAlex described as of March 2025. The authors define machine learning as 1980–2014, deep learning as 2015–2022 and generative AI as 2023 onward. Their recent-era replication uses 4,797,614 papers published during that era; this is a publication-period subset, not exclusively papers using generative models. They report consistent impact, focus and engagement patterns but explicitly cannot replicate career-transition analysis within the short generative-AI period. Selection is limited to English-language journal and conference papers with complete titles and abstracts in six natural-science disciplines. AI identification misses subtle or unmentioned use. Leadership is proxied by last authorship, while academic exit is inferred from publication inactivity, principally a three-year threshold; uncertain ultimate career status is excluded. The authors’ forward-looking recommendations have no specified implementation date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are natural scientists, junior and established team members, scientific communities and science-policy institutions; benefits are unevenly distributed.
pts.d: The studied disciplines are biology, medicine, chemistry, physics, materials science and geology. Individual adopters gain output, recognition and faster movement into leadership, while AI teams contain proportionally fewer juniors. Collective research communities face narrower topical coverage, less citation-based engagement and recognition concentrated on superstar papers. Data-poor foundational questions are identified as potentially neglected. Supplementary demographic analyses report that adoption-associated reductions in dropout are less pronounced in Africa and South America than in regions such as Asia-Pacific and North America, less pronounced for Black researchers than White and Asian or Pacific Islander researchers, and smaller for female than male researchers. Geography and institutional type are derived from affiliations; gender and ethnicity are inferred from names. The authors characterize these findings as preliminary and leave their causes and consequences open. Funders, policymakers and AI developers are addressed through the recommendation to support wider exploration. No effects on lawyers, law firms or legal markets are established or claimed.
